title: Amplify Desirable Behaviour
author: McCrea, Peps
summary: Peps McCrea argues that classroom norms operate mostly below conscious awareness yet often override formal rules and policies, which makes deliberately shaping their visibility one of the highest-leverage things a teacher can do. His central mechanism is that students infer norms primarily by observing others, so a teacher's most effective lever is narrating and highlighting the specific behaviors they want emulated — an individual student already working, a class already tracking the teacher, a story about another class's engagement — rather than issuing general rules. He adds a sharp nuance: normative messaging framed around what you want to happen works; framing it around what didn't happen (e.g., 'most of you didn't do the homework') can backfire by signaling that noncompliance is actually the norm. The piece closes by tying the timing argument directly to the start of the school year, since normative messaging is most effective in novel situations before habits calcify.
points: Norms are learned primarily by observing others, so narrating specific visible behavior ('Jem has her book out already') shapes norms more than stating rules.
Framing normative messages around what you want to happen, not what didn't happen, avoids accidentally signaling that noncompliance is the real norm.
100% visible adoption is the strongest lever — a single visible dissenter measurably weakens everyone else's pull toward the desired behavior.
Where no norm yet exists, point to an emerging one or to outcomes (a full stack of handed-in homework) as evidence of 'how things are done here.'
Normative messaging is most powerful in novel situations — the first days of a school year are the highest-leverage window before habits harden.
quotes: The presence of norms in school is inevitable—there is little we can do about it. However, the nature of these norms is within our influence.
Norms are the unwritten rules of conduct that influence behaviour and learning in school (& society). They are so powerful that they often override more formal policies and rules.

Our perceptions of norms arise predominantly from the observation of others. And so, the best way to influence norms in school is to raise the visibility of those behaviours and attitudes that we want others to emulate.

Normative messaging is more effective when it emphasises what we want to happen, rather than what we don't. Chastising a class by telling them that most students didn't do their homework can reinforce rather that deter such behaviour.
100% adoption is the ultimate lever—even a single dissenter makes it easier for us not to follow along. When we see one person picking up litter, we might consider doing it.

Normative messaging is most potent in novel situations. Once norms have taken hold, they become increasingly hard to change. This is why it is worth taking time to get things right in the early days of establishing a class.
